newsitem.title: UK: Mideast, West Africa VLCCs firm, could head higher.
newsitem.headline: Mideast, West Africa VLCCs firm, could head higher.

text.p: Middle East and West Africa very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates maintained their firm tone on Friday with signs that the market could rise further, brokers said.
"Early tonnage in both the Arabian Gulf and West Africa is extremely limited and, even up to about the 10th of next month, the situation looks fairly dire from a charterer's point of view.
"Owners are feeling fairly bullish at the moment and it is, therefore, likely that rate levels will edge up a little further," said brokers Galbraith's Ltd in their weekly report.
"The seasonal upturn which occurred towards the end of April last year, and indeed in April in 1995, has come a few weeks early this year," they added.
Mideast/Japan 250,000 tonners were fixed at about W67.5 after starting the week at W58, with older vessels fetching similar rates to Asia as modern ships, brokers said.
In the West Africa sector, the 270,000 tonne Soro was said fixed at W78.5 to UKC, Med for BP, with W85 paid for the Hellespont Orpheum for 265,000 tonnes to Canada for Shell, loading April 5.
The West Africa Suezmax (130,000 tonne) market was also strong despite the demand for VLCCs, with the Tromso Fidelity said fixed at W106.5 for 134,000 tonnes to St Croix for Hess, loading April 3.

Galbraith's said Suezmax tonnage availablity in the next three weeks "is particularly 'thin on the ground'" and although an older vessel had been agreed at W100 on a West Africa/USG voyage, "it is unlikely that anyone with earlier cargoes would be quite so lucky."
Further strength was seen in the North Sea with 80,000 tonners at W135/W140, against W115 at the end of last week.
Med Suezmaxes were firm at W107.5, mirroring the West Africa market, but 80,000 tonners were steady to softer at W107.5 on plenty of available tonnage, brokers said.

In the Caribs/upcoast sector, 70,000 tonne crude cargoes continued their recent spectacular climb over the last two weeks, hitting W205/210 against W150 at the beginning of last week. Fuel oil 50,000 tonne cargoes were at about the same level.
